newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Shooting worries North Korean defectors in Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Shooting worries North Korean defectors in Seoul.

text.p: The shooting of a prominent North Korean defector in South Korea on Saturday has sent shock waves through Seoul's community of escapees, many of whom live in fear for their lives, some of its members said on Monday.
Li Il-nam, the nephew of Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, was shot twice while standing at the doorway of a friend's home near Seoul. Police suspect the attackers were North Korean agents.
Li was critically injured and remains in a coma on life-support systems.

South Korean officials said the shooting appeared to be a warning to Seoul and potential defectors after high-ranking Pyongyang official Hwang Jang-yop sought asylum in the South Korean embassy compound in Beijing last week.

More than 600 defectors from communist North Korea live in the South. Li's shooting was the first assassination attempt on an escapee since the end of the 1950-1953 Korean War, a senior police official said.

The defectors may have left the Stalinist regime behind, but many still live in fear. Changing names is quite common in the community and many also switch addresses frequently, said Kang Chul-hwan, who came to Seoul in 1992.

"I've been told to be careful of talking to strangers on the phone since the incident, but I don't think I am the type of person a terrorist would track down," said the 29-year-old, who spent 10 years in a North Korean camp for political prisoners.
"But defectors should avoid exposure in the media, especially on television," Kang said.
After his defection in 1982, Li changed his name to Lee Han-yong and had plastic surgery to hide his identity.
But last year he basked in the media limelight after his mother, whose whereabouts are still unknown, escaped from North Korea.

Li appeared on a talk show in 1996 to reveal behind-the-scenes details of the secretive Pyongyang "royal family". He also published a book titled "Taedong River Royal Family, 14 Years Underground in Seoul," with pictures of his family and details of his life.

Since 1990 more than 200 defectors have streamed into the South. With the rise in numbers, benefits and resettlement funds have dropped drastically, and many struggle to adjust to the South's capitalist society.
"I heard Li went public to find funds for a new business," said Kang. "Life is not easy for defectors."

Publishing books, staging plays, appearing on talk shows and giving lectures have become common among defectors and an important source of income. But the recent threats by North Korea for revenge and the attack on Li could halt that.
A former North Korean spy who asked not to be named said many defectors fear for their lives since Li was shot but he doubted the attack was linked to Hwang's case.

"I used to work in the spy business, although I didn't kill, and it takes more than three days to arrange such an assassination. I think it was planned before Hwang's request for asylum," said the defector.
The government on Sunday ordered extra protection for defectors in South Korea.
"We have drawn up a list of defectors, senior officials and politicians to provide tight security against any possible terrorist attacks by North Korea," a police officer told Reuters.
